title: Thai Road Conditions by Region
excerpt: Terrain, surfaces, traffic and lighting — the physical inputs, region by region.
content:
Thailand's roads vary more than the flat-beach mental picture suggests, and the differences are physical rather than a matter of confidence. Here is what the surfaces, gradients, traffic and lighting are actually like, region by region.

The one thing that applies almost everywhere

Street lighting is poor to absent outside Bangkok and the main urban areas. Island roads, mountain roads and rural stretches are largely unlit after dark. This is the most consistent finding across every region surveyed, and it applies equally to a car, a scooter and someone walking.

Most island roads also have no footpaths. Walking between bays means sharing the carriageway with traffic, which is a daylight consideration and a considerably larger one after sunset.

Northern Thailand

Mountainous, with sharp curves and switchbacks. The roads are properly surfaced but the gradients and cornering are sustained rather than occasional.

Route 1095 between Chiang Mai and Pai is the specific stretch most often discussed. It is commonly cited as having 762 curves over roughly 135 km — a figure repeated on signage and in most accounts of the route, though it reads as a tourist landmark number rather than a survey measurement. What is not in dispute is the character: continuous mountain switchbacks, with limited lighting on the mountain sections.

Phuket

Hilly, with winding coastal and mountain roads connecting the west-coast beaches. Traffic volume is heavier than on the smaller islands, and the island is 48 to 50 km long, so distances between beaches involve real driving rather than short hops. Lighting on the connecting roads is limited.

Koh Samui

The ring road runs about 51 km around the island and is mostly flat coastal driving. The interior behind it is hilly, and the access roads climbing to interior viewpoints and resorts are steeper than the ring itself suggests. Lighting on the ring road is limited outside the built-up stretches.

The smaller southern islands

Mixed. Main roads are generally paved and in reasonable condition, and the surfacing has improved considerably in recent years. What varies is what happens off the main road.

On Koh Tao, one wide paved road connects Sairee, Mae Haad and Chalok Baan Kao, with side roads of similar quality running over to east-coast bays like Hin Wong, Tanote and Sai Daeng. Some dirt tracks remain in more remote areas, and some destinations need four-wheel drive to reach. The terrain between bays is hilly.

Koh Lanta is long and narrow with beaches along the west coast, and Koh Phangan spreads across multiple bays — in both cases the main coastal roads are paved, with the variation sitting in the access roads down to individual beaches.

Bangkok

Flat, dense, and the one place with reliably good street lighting in the urban core. Traffic volume rather than road surface is the governing condition.

Who shares the road

One characteristic that does not appear on a map: in the tourist areas, road users come from many countries with different driving conventions. Rules that are automatic in one place are unfamiliar in another, and the mix is at its most varied on the islands where rental vehicles are most common.

Roads are also shared with pedestrians and animals in the absence of footpaths, which is the practical reason the lighting question matters as much as it does.

What the law requires on these roads

Two rules travel with the conditions above. Helmets are legally required for both rider and passenger, and riding a motorbike legally needs a motorcycle licence from your home country plus an International Driving Permit — both, not either.

Enforcement is the part that misleads. Police checkpoints are common in tourist areas, and being stopped without the right permit or helmet typically means a fine of a few hundred baht, commonly in the region of 400 to 500. Travellers who have been stopped once tend to conclude the whole issue is minor.

The fine is not the risk. Many travel policies exclude a motorbike claim where the rider held no valid motorcycle licence or was not wearing a helmet — and on an unlit road with no footpath, that exclusion meets exactly the conditions this page describes. Our guide to renting a car or scooter sets out the licence chain in full.

How the physical picture fits the rest

Terrain, surfacing, traffic and lighting are inputs rather than answers. What they mean depends on how far you need to travel on any given day, what transport alternatives exist where you are staying, and whether the journeys in question happen in daylight.

How the road conditions combine with distances and transport coverage for a particular itinerary is worked through in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

Are Thai roads well lit at night?

Outside Bangkok and the main urban areas, generally not. Island roads, mountain roads and rural stretches are largely unlit, and most island roads have no footpaths.

How difficult is the road from Chiang Mai to Pai?

It is continuous mountain driving — commonly cited as 762 curves over roughly 135 km, with sharp switchbacks and limited lighting on the mountain sections. The surface itself is properly made.

What are the roads like on Koh Tao?

One wide paved road connects the three main villages, with side roads of similar quality to the east-coast bays. Some dirt tracks remain in remote areas and some spots require four-wheel drive. The terrain between bays is hilly.

Is Phuket hilly?

Yes — winding coastal and mountain roads connect the west-coast beaches, and at 48 to 50 km long the distances between them involve real driving rather than short hops.

Do Thai island roads have sidewalks?

Mostly not. Walking between bays means sharing the carriageway with traffic, which matters most where lighting is absent after dark.

title: Medical Care in Thailand: What Exists Where
excerpt: Bangkok and a small island are different countries medically. What each tier offers, and how payment works.
content:
Thailand has a well-developed medical system, and what a visitor encounters depends heavily on where they are when they need it. Bangkok and a small island are different countries medically. Here is what exists, what it costs, and how payment works.

Public and private

Thailand runs both systems, and foreign visitors overwhelmingly use the private one.

Private hospitals cost more, generally have English-speaking staff, and have shorter waits. Several in Bangkok are set up specifically for international patients, with dedicated international departments.

Public hospitals cost considerably less, have longer waits, and English varies with the institution and the individual. They are not inferior medically — Thailand's public system handles the country's population — but they are not organised around foreign visitors.

What exists where

The tier of care available drops sharply outside the main centres, and this is the fact worth knowing before you need it.

Bangkok has multiple internationally accredited private hospitals with full specialist departments — the top tier of care in the region.

Phuket and Koh Samui have full private hospitals capable of handling serious cases.

Koh Phangan, Koh Tao, Koh Lanta and Koh Chang have clinics or basic facilities rather than full hospitals. They can handle ordinary problems — infections, minor injuries, stomach trouble — and they stabilise rather than treat anything serious.

That last distinction is the one that matters. A clinic on a small island is a first response, not a destination. Anything beyond its scope means a transfer, which our guide to medical evacuation from Thai islands covers.

How payment works

Private hospitals typically require payment, or a guarantee of payment from an insurer, before non-emergency treatment. This surprises Americans used to being treated first and billed later.

A guarantee of payment is a document the insurer issues to the specific hospital, arranged through the insurer's assistance line. Without one, the patient pays and claims back afterwards — which means having the funds available at the time. Our guide to what travel insurance actually covers goes through that mechanic in detail.

Pharmacies

Thai pharmacies operate with a wider scope than American ones. Many medications that require a prescription in the United States are available over the counter, and pharmacists routinely advise on minor complaints.

For a visitor this cuts two ways: minor problems that would need a doctor's appointment at home can often be handled at a pharmacy counter, and medications that are tightly controlled at home may be easier to obtain than expected. What a pharmacy can dispense varies, and anything requiring a diagnosis is still a doctor's job.

Continuing a prescription

Refilling a US prescription in Thailand generally requires a consultation with a local doctor, who issues a Thai prescription. Bringing the original prescription and keeping medication in its labelled packaging makes that process straightforward.

Emergency numbers

The nationwide medical emergency number is 1669.

The Tourist Police line, 1155, is English-speaking and is frequently the more practical first call for a visitor who does not speak Thai — they can translate and coordinate. For a genuine medical emergency, 1669 is the number; for anything where the language barrier is itself the obstacle, 1155 is worth knowing.

What it costs

Private care in Thailand is inexpensive by American standards for small things and expensive in absolute terms for large ones, and the gap between those two is where travellers get caught.

A pharmacy consultation or a clinic visit for an infection or a stomach upset is the kind of sum you would not think twice about at home. A serious injury requiring surgery at a private hospital runs into the tens of thousands of US dollars, and a medical evacuation off a small island runs into five figures on top of that.

Neither number is the reason to worry — the reason is the payment order described below. A hospital that wants a guarantee of payment before treating you is asking a question your insurer answers, not your credit card, provided the call was made in time. Two things Americans routinely assume cover them generally do not: US domestic health insurance provides little or no coverage abroad, and credit-card travel benefits are usually thinner than a dedicated policy.

What this connects to

Where you are staying determines what medical tier you are near, what an emergency transfer would involve, and how much a policy's evacuation coverage matters. Those are three separate things that get decided at three separate times — accommodation weeks out, insurance in a single sitting, and the emergency, if it comes, without warning.

How the medical picture connects to the base and island decisions is worked through in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

What is the emergency number in Thailand?

1669 for medical emergencies nationwide. The Tourist Police line, 1155, is English-speaking and is often the more practical first call for a visitor facing a language barrier.

Do Thai hospitals treat you before payment?

Private hospitals typically require payment or a guarantee of payment from an insurer before non-emergency treatment. A guarantee is arranged through the insurer's assistance line, not by the hospital.

Is there a hospital on Koh Tao?

Koh Tao has clinics rather than a full hospital. Koh Samui and Phuket have full private hospitals; Koh Phangan, Koh Lanta and Koh Chang have clinic-level facilities.

Can I buy medication over the counter in Thailand?

Thai pharmacies dispense many medications that require a prescription in the United States, and pharmacists advise on minor complaints. Anything requiring a diagnosis still needs a doctor.

Can I refill a US prescription in Thailand?

Generally through a consultation with a local doctor who issues a Thai prescription. Bringing the original prescription and keeping medication in labelled packaging helps.

title: Bangkok Has Two Airports: The Transfer Between Them
excerpt: About 50 km apart, 45 minutes to 2.5 hours by road, no rail link, and no official minimum connection time.
content:
Bangkok has two airports about 50 km apart, and travellers routinely book an international arrival at one and a domestic departure from the other without noticing. Here is what moving between them actually involves.

Which airport is which

Suvarnabhumi (BKK) handles full-service and most international carriers. If you are flying in from the United States, this is almost certainly where you land.

Don Mueang (DMK) handles primarily low-cost carriers, including a large share of the domestic network. If you booked a cheap flight to Phuket or Chiang Mai separately, there is a good chance it leaves from here.

They are separate airports roughly 50 km apart by road, not two terminals of the same place.

How long the transfer takes

Off-peak, the road transfer runs 45 to 60 minutes. In Bangkok traffic it runs 90 minutes to two and a half hours.

That spread is the fact worth carrying. The same journey can take three times as long depending on the hour, and the hour is set by when your inbound flight lands rather than by anything you choose.

There is no rail link between them

The Airport Rail Link connects Suvarnabhumi to the city. It does not reach Don Mueang. Any transfer between the two airports is a road journey and is subject to road conditions.

The free shuttle, and who cannot use it

Airports of Thailand runs a free shuttle bus between the two airports, roughly 05:00 to midnight, taking around 50 minutes in normal traffic.

The eligibility rule is stricter than it first appears. The service is exclusively for passengers transferring between the two airports — a boarding pass or e-ticket for an onward flight and a passport must be shown at the counter. The airport authority states plainly that non-connecting passengers and the general public are not eligible.

So someone spending a night in the city between two flights is not a transferring passenger by this definition, and pays for their own transport in both directions.

Where it goes from

At Suvarnabhumi, the shuttle leaves from Level 2 (arrivals), Gate 3, where a desk checks flight details. At Don Mueang, the shuttle counter sits inside the terminal near exit 6, and check-in there happens before going out to the stop.

What an international-to-domestic connection involves

None of this happens airside. An arriving international passenger:

  • Clears immigration
  • Reclaims checked baggage
  • Exits to landside
  • Travels 50 km across Bangkok
  • Checks in again from scratch at the other airport

It is a complete re-entry into the system, not a transfer within one. Bags are not through-checked between separately booked tickets, which is the mechanical reason each step has to be repeated.

No official minimum connection time

Airlines publish minimum connection times for connections within an airport. For a connection between Suvarnabhumi and Don Mueang, no official minimum is published at all.

That absence is itself the fact. Various figures circulate in guides and forums, and none of them carries any authority — there is no airport or airline standard being cited. What exists instead is the arithmetic above: immigration, baggage, a road journey that varies between 45 minutes and 2.5 hours, and a fresh check-in.

What to do about it

There are only three honest answers, and the first two are decided at booking.

Put both legs on one ticket. Then the airline owns the connection, your bag is through-checked, and none of the arithmetic above is yours.

Or give the gap a night. Sleep in Bangkok and fly south the next morning. This is the option that survives a delayed transpacific arrival, and it is cheaper than the replacement ticket a missed separately-booked flight costs.

Or, if you must connect the same day, arrive early and not late. The road leg is the variable, and the variable is set by the clock: a mid-afternoon landing puts the transfer into Bangkok's worst traffic, where the same 50 km takes two and a half hours instead of forty-five minutes.

Where this decision actually gets made

Almost nobody chooses this transfer deliberately. It arrives as a consequence — the international ticket was booked for price and schedule, the domestic leg was booked separately weeks later, and the two airports were never the same field in either search.

How the airport split interacts with the rest of an itinerary is worked through in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

How far apart are Bangkok's two airports?

About 50 km by road. Suvarnabhumi (BKK) handles international and full-service carriers; Don Mueang (DMK) handles primarily low-cost and domestic flights.

How long does the BKK to DMK transfer take?

45 to 60 minutes off-peak, and 90 minutes to two and a half hours in traffic.

Is there a free shuttle between Bangkok's airports?

Yes, run by Airports of Thailand, roughly 05:00 to midnight. It is exclusively for passengers transferring between the two airports — a boarding pass for an onward flight and a passport are required, and non-connecting passengers are not eligible.

Can I take a train between the two airports?

No. The Airport Rail Link serves Suvarnabhumi and the city but does not reach Don Mueang, so any transfer is a road journey.

What is the minimum connection time between BKK and DMK?

There is no official published minimum. What exists is the process: immigration, baggage reclaim, a road transfer of 45 minutes to 2.5 hours, and a fresh check-in.

title: Domestic Flight or Overnight Train in Thailand
excerpt: An hour in the air against thirteen in a berth — and what each does to the day around it.
content:
Bangkok to Chiang Mai, or Bangkok toward the southern islands, can be covered by air in about an hour or by sleeper train overnight. They are not the same journey in any respect except the endpoints. Here is what each involves.

The flight

Bangkok to Chiang Mai takes about an hour in the air. Bangkok to Phuket runs about an hour and fifteen minutes; to Koh Samui about an hour.

Domestic routes are operated by Thai Airways, Bangkok Airways, Thai AirAsia, Nok Air and Thai Lion Air. Which airport a flight leaves from depends on the carrier — the low-cost airlines operate largely from Don Mueang, the full-service ones from Suvarnabhumi, and those are two separate airports about 50 km apart.

The hour in the air is not the journey. Airport travel at both ends, check-in, security and baggage reclaim surround it, and where the departure airport is not the one you arrived into, a 50 km road transfer surrounds that.

The overnight train

Sleepers run north to Chiang Mai and south toward Surat Thani, the mainland gateway for the Gulf islands.

Bangkok to Chiang Mai takes about 12.5 to 13 hours, with services departing in the evening and arriving early the following morning.

Bangkok toward Surat Thani takes about 11 to 13 hours.

Accommodation is in first or second class air-conditioned sleepers with upper and lower berths; fan-cooled options exist on some services. Popular berths need booking weeks ahead.

The station changed

Long-distance services in all directions now run from Krung Thep Aphiwat Central Terminal. Hua Lamphong, the station named in most older guides and still fixed in a lot of published itineraries, is no longer the primary long-distance terminus.

Anyone planning from a guide written before the change would arrive at the wrong station.

What each does to the day around it

This is where the two diverge most, and it has nothing to do with the journey time.

A flight consumes part of a day at both ends — travel to the airport, the flight, travel from it. The day it lands in is a partial day.

An overnight train consumes a night and arrives early in the morning. It also removes a night of accommodation from the trip, and delivers a traveller into a full day at the destination rather than a partial one — though a full day begun on whatever sleep the berth allowed.

So the comparison is not one hour against thirteen. It is a partial day plus a hotel night, against a night in a berth and a full day on the ground.

Booking mechanics

Sleeper berths sell out weeks in advance on popular routes, so the train is the leg that has to be committed to early. Domestic flights are generally available closer in, at fares that move with demand.

Fares for both move enough that they are worth checking live rather than planning against a remembered figure:

100 USD ≈ … THB (enable JavaScript for today's rate)

Where the train does not go

One limit is worth stating plainly, because the comparison above only holds on the routes where both options exist.

The sleeper serves Chiang Mai in the north and Surat Thani in the south. Surat Thani is a mainland town, not an island — it is the gateway for the Gulf islands, and reaching Koh Samui, Koh Phangan or Koh Tao from it still means a bus-and-boat or ferry transfer on top of the overnight journey.

For Phuket and Krabi there is no equivalent choice at all: neither is on the rail network, so the comparison there is a flight against a long overland bus, which is a different question from the one on this page.

Where this sits in a trip

The choice looks like a transport question and behaves like an itinerary question. It determines which day the destination begins, whether a hotel night is spent in Bangkok or in a berth, how early one leg has to be committed, and — if the flight leaves from the other airport — whether a 50 km road transfer sits in the middle of it.

Those consequences land in different parts of the plan and are decided at different times. How they fit together is worked through in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

How long is the overnight train from Bangkok to Chiang Mai?

About 12.5 to 13 hours, departing in the evening and arriving early the next morning.

Which Bangkok station do long-distance trains leave from?

Krung Thep Aphiwat Central Terminal serves all long-distance directions. Hua Lamphong, named in most older guides, is no longer the primary long-distance terminus.

How far ahead do I need to book a sleeper berth?

Weeks ahead on popular routes. Domestic flights are generally available closer to the date, at fares that move with demand.

How long is the flight from Bangkok to Chiang Mai?

About an hour in the air, with airport time at both ends — and a 50 km road transfer if the departure airport is not the one you arrived into.

What classes are on Thai sleeper trains?

First and second class air-conditioned sleepers with upper and lower berths, plus fan-cooled options on some services.

title: Thai Domestic Flights: Baggage, Changes and Separate Tickets
excerpt: Carry-on-only fares, through-checking rules, and why a separately booked leg carries no protection at all.
content:
A cheap domestic fare in Thailand often prices differently once a bag and a schedule change are added, and a leg booked separately from the international ticket carries no protection at all. Here is how the mechanics work.

Baggage allowance

The allowance depends on which kind of carrier you booked.

Full-service carriers — Thai Airways, Bangkok Airways — typically include 20 to 30 kg of checked baggage in the fare.

Low-cost carriers — Thai AirAsia, Nok Air, Thai Lion Air — commonly sell carry-on-only fares, with checked baggage as a paid add-on bought at booking or later at a higher price.

This matters more on a Thailand trip than on a short break, because arriving from the United States generally means checked luggage. A carry-on-only domestic fare and a transpacific suitcase are not compatible, and the add-on bought at the airport costs more than the same add-on bought at booking.

Through-checked baggage

Baggage is through-checked to the final destination on a single ticket, and between codeshare partners on a connected itinerary.

It is not through-checked across separately booked tickets. Two separate bookings mean reclaiming bags at the intermediate airport and checking them in again for the next leg — which is also why a connection between Bangkok's two airports involves a full re-entry into the system rather than a transfer.

Changes and cancellations

Change and cancellation fees vary by fare class and by how close to departure the change is made. The cheapest fares are commonly non-refundable, and on low-cost carriers a change fee plus a fare difference can approach the price of a new ticket.

The fare class is where this is decided, at booking, usually before anyone knows whether the schedule will hold.

The separately booked leg

This is the mechanic with the largest consequence and the least visibility.

When a domestic leg is booked separately from the international ticket, neither airline has any obligation to the other's passenger. If the inbound long-haul is delayed and the domestic connection is missed, there is no rebooking, no compensation, and no protection. The domestic ticket is simply forfeited and a new one has to be bought.

The same structure applies in reverse at the end of a trip: a delayed domestic flight that causes a missed international departure is the traveller's problem, not the carrier's.

This is identical in structure to what happens when a ferry cancellation strands someone before a flight — separate bookings are separate contracts, and weather or delay is nobody's fault, which makes it yours.

Koh Samui is a special case

Koh Samui's airport is privately owned and operated by Bangkok Airways, which limits which carriers serve it. Fewer operators means fewer alternatives if a flight is missed or cancelled — a different situation from Phuket or Krabi, where several carriers compete on the same routes.

The basket that looks like one ticket

The distinction between one ticket and two is the whole of the section above, which makes it worth knowing how the two are told apart — because a booking site will happily sell you two and show you one confirmation.

A single ticket, or a connection between codeshare partners on one itinerary, carries one booking reference for the whole journey and through-checks the bag to the final destination. Two tickets sold together in one basket carry two separate references, and everything in the section above applies: no protection, no through-checking, and a forfeited fare if the first leg runs late.

The reference count is the test, and it is visible on the confirmation email before you fly rather than at a check-in desk after you land.

Where these mechanics land

Baggage rules, fare class and booking structure are all settled at the moment of purchase, typically weeks or months out, and typically in a search that optimises for headline price. What each one costs only becomes visible later — at a check-in desk, or in the gap between a delayed arrival and a departure that has already closed.

How the booking structure interacts with the shape of an itinerary is worked through in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

Do Thai domestic flights include checked baggage?

Full-service carriers typically include 20 to 30 kg. Low-cost carriers commonly sell carry-on-only fares with checked baggage as a paid add-on, cheaper at booking than at the airport.

Will my bags be checked through to my final destination?

On a single ticket or between codeshare partners, yes. Across separately booked tickets, no — bags must be reclaimed and re-checked.

What happens if a delay makes me miss a separately booked domestic flight?

Neither airline has any obligation to you. There is no rebooking or compensation — the domestic ticket is forfeited and a new one has to be bought.

Can I change a Thai domestic flight?

Fees vary by fare class and timing, and the cheapest fares are commonly non-refundable. On low-cost carriers a change fee plus fare difference can approach the cost of a new ticket.

Why do fewer airlines fly to Koh Samui?

The airport is privately owned and operated by Bangkok Airways, which limits which carriers serve it — and so limits the alternatives if a flight is missed.

title: Getting to the Southern Islands by Air
excerpt: Four southern airports, and the islands that have none — which journeys are one leg and which are three.
content:
Four of Thailand's southern islands have an airport. The rest are reached by a flight to somewhere else, a road transfer, and a boat. Which category an island falls into shapes every journey to and from it.

The airports and what they actually serve

Phuket (HKT) and Koh Samui (USM) serve their own islands directly. Land and you are there.

Krabi (KBV) serves the Krabi and Ao Nang area on the mainland, which is where many people stay while visiting the surrounding islands by day boat.

Surat Thani (URT) is a mainland airport and the gateway for the Gulf islands. It is not on an island and no island is walkable from it.

Flights from Bangkok run about an hour to Koh Samui and about an hour and fifteen minutes to Phuket.

The islands with no airport

Koh Phangan, Koh Tao, Koh Lanta and Koh Chang have no airport at all. Reaching any of them means flying to a mainland or larger-island airport, transferring by road to the relevant pier, and taking a boat.

So a journey to Koh Tao is a flight, a road transfer, and a crossing — three legs, each with its own timetable, most often booked separately from one another.

What that means when something goes wrong

These are the same four islands that have clinics rather than hospitals, and Koh Tao and Koh Phangan are among the crossings most frequently suspended in rough weather. Three separate pieces of information, arrived at independently, describing the same set of places.

Koh Samui's airport is unusual

Koh Samui airport is privately owned and operated by Bangkok Airways, which limits which carriers serve it. The island with the most direct air access has the most constrained set of operators on that access, which means fewer alternatives when a flight is cancelled or missed.

Seasonal schedules

Domestic schedules to the southern airports thin out outside high season. Fewer daily services means fewer options on any given day, and the reduced season overlaps with the wetter months when boat crossings are also more likely to be disrupted.

What is not published

Last departure times from the southern airports are not reliably documented. That gap matters more than it sounds, because it is the fact that determines whether a same-day connection from an international arrival is possible at all — whether a traveller landing in Bangkok in the afternoon can reach a southern island that night, or is spending it in Bangkok.

Anyone quoting a confident last-flight time is working from a schedule that may have changed. The current timetable for the specific date is the only reliable source.

The return is the harder direction

Everything above describes the journey out. The same legs run in reverse at the end of the trip, and that is the direction that costs something, because an international departure is waiting at the end of them.

Going out, a delayed boat costs you an afternoon. Coming back, the same delay runs through a road transfer and a domestic flight before it reaches a long-haul ticket that was almost certainly booked separately — and a separately booked leg carries no protection at all. The undocumented last departure times matter most here: the question is not whether a boat runs that day but whether the one you need still connects.

The practical answer is to come back a day early and spend the last night on the mainland or in Bangkok. It converts the whole chain from a risk into a buffer, and it is the one decision on this page that costs nothing to make in advance.

Where the air map sits in a trip

Which islands have airports, which need a boat, how many legs each journey involves, and how those legs are booked are all fixed facts, knowable while an itinerary is being built. They interact with when the international flight lands, how the domestic leg was booked, and which season the trip falls in — none of which is decided at the same moment.

How the southern air map combines with the rest of an itinerary is worked through in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

Which Thai islands have airports?

Phuket (HKT) and Koh Samui (USM) have airports on the island itself. Krabi (KBV) serves the mainland Krabi and Ao Nang area, and Surat Thani (URT) is the mainland gateway for the Gulf islands.

How do I get to Koh Tao?

There is no airport. It means flying to a mainland or larger-island airport, transferring by road to the pier, and taking a boat — three legs, usually booked separately.

How long is the flight from Bangkok to Koh Samui?

About an hour. Phuket is about an hour and fifteen minutes.

Do flights to southern Thailand run year-round?

Yes, but schedules thin out outside high season — which overlaps with the wetter months when boat crossings are also more likely to be disrupted.

Can I reach a southern island the same day I land in Bangkok?

It depends on the last departure of the day, which is not reliably published and varies by airport and season. The current timetable for your specific date is the only reliable source.
